works.name: m4Bookmaker
works.hero: You own what you can hold, file by file, on your own machine.
works.short_description: A desktop app that converts folders of MP3 (or other audio) files into clean, properly chaptered M4B audiobooks you own outright.
substantive_description: A small app with a large argument. m4Bookmaker exists because Audible's ecosystem treats audiobook ownership as a license rather than a possession — a contract that can be revoked, a format that will not move, a library that lives on someone else's server at someone else's discretion. The technical solution is small — rebuild the M4B yourself from MP3s — and the position is large: you own what you can hold, file by file, on your own machine. The full pipeline handles automatic chapter detection from filenames, an interactive visual chapter editor with a built-in audio player, batch queue processing, and automatic repair of common encoding problems, with a deliberate GUI-to-CLI symmetry that keeps it scriptable without sacrificing approachability. It was one of the first tools built under the Ho System — concept to signed, packaged, distributed product in 3.5 days — and the position it embodies is structural: every time a tool gets repossessed by its platform, a small piece of personal capacity dies, and m4Bookmaker is the refusal of that pattern, sized to one specific failure.
Python with PyQt5 and FFmpeg; shipped as a signed macOS app and a Windows installer, and distributed as a PyPI package.

relationships.note: One of the first Ho System builds: concept to signed, packaged, distributed product in 3.5 days.

state.last: Full security/correctness/optimization review of the codebase, then all findings fixed across four commits (`c518f54` core hardening: M4BError exception layer replacing library sys.exit, atomic encode via .partial + os.replace, FFMETADATA escaping, narrator ©nrt/©wrt fix incl. the reported "narrator not saved" bug (root cause: comment tag masked the saved composer atom on reload), post-repair chapter retiming, codec-uniformity check, probe caching; `328b2ee` build supply chain: SHA-256 pin on the third-party ffmpeg zip, hash-locked requirements-build.lock, entitlements documented; `d90d7ba` GUI thread lifecycle: quit/close cancels+waits workers, queue Stop→Start race fixed, bound-method signal connections (fatal quit-during-load crash), stylesheet quadratic-repolish fix; `dcef544` GUI edit-mode/widgets: timeline-preserving chapter remove, time edits honoured on Convert, output-path sanitization, async pickers/downloads, player seek-timer + release-before-save). Verification: 992 tests green (~10s), coverage 90% total, mypy 54→30 (rest is pre-existing window.py debt), live E2E smoke with hostile metadata passed.
state.next: finish 1.1.0 release: test the DMG by launching it, test the Windows installer from the CI artifact, publish the draft GitHub Release (this triggers in-app update notifications), upload both installers to Payhip, close issue #20 referencing 1.1.0.
state.holdup: Released so far: PyPI 1.1.0 live; tag v1.1.0 pushed (merge commit f357cb6, PR #21); signed+notarized+stapled DMG attached to DRAFT GitHub release. Two hash-locked-build lessons committed: static_ffmpeg 3.0 stdout chatter (SF_DIR capture) and Pillow 11 has no universal2 wheels (excluded from bundle — app ships Pillow-free as 1.0.5 did). Open bugs NOT in this release: #15/#16 "output marked Protected" (DRM-origin metadata via -map_metadata) — candidate next ho. Hygiene ho candidate: ~30 window.py mypy-strict errors, 15 E501s. Entitlements re-test on next PyInstaller/PySide6 major bump.
